name: Amisulpride
sections: Developed in France as a substituted benzamide related to sulpiride; patents expired by 2008 and generic versions are widely available. First approval/introduction: Introduced in the 1990s (Sanofi-Synthélabo); not approved as an antipsychotic in the USA (IV form approved 2020 as an antiemetic).

Selective dopamine D2/D3 receptor antagonist with preferential limbic action. At low doses (50–300 mg/day) it blocks presynaptic D2/D3 autoreceptors, increasing dopamine release (useful for negative symptoms and dysthymia); at higher doses (400–1200 mg/day) it blocks postsynaptic receptors, controlling positive symptoms. Receptor / target profile: Dopamine D2/D3 antagonist (Ki 3.0/3.5 nM); also potent 5-HT7 antagonist (Ki 11.5 nM), which may contribute to antidepressant effects.
Minimal hepatic metabolism; mostly excreted unchanged

Summary: Oral bioavailability ~48%; two absorption peaks (1 h and 3–4 h). Low protein binding (~16%). Minimal metabolism; excreted largely unchanged in urine. Elimination half-life ~12 h. Dose reduction needed in renal impairment.
Acute and chronic schizophrenia with predominantly positive symptoms (delusions, hallucinations, thought disorder)
Schizophrenia with predominantly negative symptoms (affective flattening, emotional and social withdrawal)
Low dose: dysthymia (off-label in some regions)
Predominantly negative symptoms: 50–300 mg once daily
Acute psychotic episodes: 400–800 mg/day in two divided doses (max 1200 mg/day)
Doses up to 300 mg may be taken once daily; higher doses in two divided doses
Renal impairment: CrCl 30–60 mL/min – half dose; 10–30 mL/min – one-third dose
Not recommended in children under 15 years
Dose to be individualised by the treating physician according to clinical response and tolerability.
CrCl 30–60: ½ dose; 10–30: ⅓ dose; <10: avoid (no data).
Increased sensitivity to hypotension and sedation; stroke risk with dementia – use cautiously.
Contraindicated before puberty; not recommended under 18 years.
Limited data; use only if clearly needed. Neonates exposed in the third trimester may show extrapyramidal and/or withdrawal symptoms.
Excreted in breast milk; breastfeeding not recommended.
Prolactin-dependent tumours (e.g. pituitary prolactinoma, breast cancer)
Concomitant levodopa or drugs that prolong QT / cause torsades de pointes
Dose-dependent QT prolongation – caution with bradycardia, hypokalaemia, congenital long QT
Increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis; stroke risk
Lowers seizure threshold; venous thromboembolism risk
Reduce dose in renal impairment (CrCl 30–60: half dose; 10–30: one-third)
Raised prolactin, breast pain, menstrual disturbance, sexual dysfunction
QT-prolonging drugs: class IA/III antiarrhythmics, some macrolides, antipsychotics, methadone
Take with or without food; avoid alcohol.
ECG (QTc) at baseline in at-risk patients; electrolytes (K, Mg); prolactin if symptomatic; weight, glucose and lipids.
Exaggerated pharmacological effects: drowsiness, sedation, hypotension, extrapyramidal symptoms, coma. Supportive care with ECG monitoring; not significantly removed by haemodialysis.
Leucht et al., Lancet 2013 – network meta-analysis of 15 antipsychotics: amisulpride ranked among the most efficacious with low weight-gain liability.
EUFEST (Kahn et al., Lancet 2008) – first-episode schizophrenia: amisulpride had lower all-cause discontinuation than haloperidol.
May cause breast enlargement, milk discharge or missed periods – report these
Do not drive until you know how it affects you
Report palpitations, fainting, high fever with stiffness
Store below 30°C in a dry place, protected from light and moisture. Keep out of the reach of children. Do not use after the expiry date.
